slots.practicalActivity: Write and run make_data.py exactly as specified to generate harvest_table.db (a seeded, synthetic SQLite database for the fictional meal-kit company Harvest Table), and confirm the printed counts match exactly: {'customers': 4040, 'orders': 140643, 'tickets': 4351, 'cancellations': 878}, churn_rate_window 0.142. Then run the 5 documented audit queries against the database and confirm you find the same 5 quirks the lesson found: 40 duplicate customer rows, 16 spellings of 4 regions, 159 missing and 12 impossible ages, 855 non-ISO signup dates, and 1,406 dollar-sign order amounts plus 300 missing discounts.
slots.deliverable: A generated harvest_table.db reproducing the exact documented row counts and churn rate, plus a written quirks log recording all 5 data-quality problems with their exact counts, ready to be fixed in the next two lessons.

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the 5 scoping questions (decision, unit of prediction, snapshot timing, label and window, population) for the Harvest Table retention request, then write and run the SQL label query against harvest_table.db, confirming it returns exactly 3,690 active customers with 568 churning in the next 60 days (a 15.4% base rate). Run the leakage-check query that finds orders dated after the 2025-06-30 snapshot, confirming the same 371 "future" orders the lesson found, and write the one-page assumptions document (population, label, output, capacity, features) to send to a stakeholder.
slots.deliverable: The executed label SQL returning 3,690 active customers and 568 churners, the leakage-check query output isolating 371 future-dated orders, and a written one-page scoping-assumptions document.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the cost model in Python (contact cost $15, a 30% save rate, $240 value per saved customer) to derive the 20.8% break-even precision, and confirm that contacting every active customer or a random 10% both lose money under these assumptions. Then build and run the random-scorer evaluation harness (average precision, ROC AUC, precision@k, lift) and confirm it lands at the floor exactly as the lesson found (AP near 0.159, AUC near 0.514, precision@k near 0.154, lift near 1.0), and write the acceptance criteria (minimum viable, beat the baselines, ambition target left open, honest validation plan) before any modeling begins.
slots.deliverable: The printed break-even calculation and net-value table for 4 precision scenarios, the random-scorer harness output proving the known floor, and a written acceptance-criteria document to hold every later model against.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's window-function deduplication check (confirming 4,000 distinct customers 2 independent ways), then expose the text-column trap by averaging the raw amount column against a CAST-and-strip version and confirming the same 1,406-row swing the lesson found. Write and run the full CTE-based extract.sql with a :snap parameter joining population, label, order features, and ticket features, confirming it returns exactly 3,690 rows with 568 churners, a minimum recency_days of 0, and no future orders leaking in.
slots.deliverable: A working extract.sql producing the leakage-safe 3,690-row, 15-column feature table, with printed sanity checks (row count, churner count, minimum recency) matching the lesson's documented numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: Write clean.py implementing all 6 documented cleaning rules (deduplicate on customer_id, parse 3 signup-date formats, standardize region casing, median-impute impossible ages, strip dollar signs from amounts, fill missing discounts with 0), run it, and confirm every before/after count matches the lesson (4,040 to 4,000 rows; 16 to 4 region spellings; 170 ages imputed at a median of 38; 1,406 dollar-sign strings fixed; 300 discounts filled). Then reconcile your Python-computed population, label, and 3 behavior features against the SQL extract from the previous lesson, confirming they agree exactly except for one documented fillna difference.
slots.deliverable: A working clean.py with every rule's before/after count printed, plus a reconciliation script proving the population, label, and 3 behavior features computed independently in SQL and pandas agree, with the one known discrepancy explained.

slots.practicalActivity: Build frame.py's one-row-per-active-customer exploration table (order_rate, tenure_days, bad_share, orders_90d, recency, avg_amount, tickets_90d), rank the numeric signals with a Spearman correlation against churn, and draw the categorical churn-rate chart (plan, channel, region, each with 95% error bars against the 15.4% average) and the 4-panel behavior-band chart. Run the 2x2 tenure-by-late-share cross table and confirm churn roughly triples from the safest corner to the riskiest, exactly as the lesson found.
slots.deliverable: The exploration table with its Spearman-ranked signal list, the categorical and behavior-band charts with their underlying numbers, and the 2x2 crossed-signal table showing the compounding risk effect.

lessons.title: Findings So Far: A Checkpoint Review

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the 5 pipeline-reverification assertions (one row per customer, 3,690 active customers, 568 churners, no future orders, no nulls in key columns) and confirm all 5 print PASS. Run chi-square tests on the 3 categorical columns and Mann-Whitney tests on the 7 numeric columns against churn, price the "tenure over a year and over 10% late/refunded" segment using the lesson 3 economics (confirming roughly 874 customers at 27.3% churn and about $4,098 of expected net value), log the data quirks table, and write the full checkpoint memo (what was done, found, not known, risks, next).
slots.deliverable: A 5-check PASS verification script, the full hypothesis-test table with chi-square and Mann-Whitney p-values, the priced high-risk segment calculation, and a written checkpoint memo ready to send to a stakeholder.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend build_frame() into build_features(), adding orders_30d, the 30-vs-prior-60-day trend, discount_share, and avg_resolution_hrs, save the resulting 3,690-row, 16-column features.csv, and run the leakage checklist in writing. Perform the stratified 80/20 split (sealing the test set until the evaluation lesson) and run the baseline comparison — the churn-rate dummy, the "days since last order" rule, the "fewest orders per week" rule, and logistic regression — confirming the documented top-10%-precision progression of roughly 0.153, 0.183, 0.268, and 0.390, then set the ambition target at 0.32 with a written justification.
slots.deliverable: The saved features.csv and sealed train/test split, a 4-row baseline comparison table (rule vs. precision@10%), and a written one-sentence justification for the 0.32 ambition target set only after seeing the baselines.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the churn-rate dummy, logistic regression, a random forest, and histogram gradient boosting through identical RepeatedStratifiedKFold (5 splits x 3 repeats) cross-validation with one shared preprocessing pipeline, comparing average precision, AUC, and precision@10% across all 4. Run the paired fold-by-fold comparison of the forest and the boosting model against logistic regression (mean delta and fold win-count), and decide which 2 models you are carrying into tuning.
slots.deliverable: A 4-model cross-validated metrics table, the paired-difference comparison showing mean AP delta and fold win-counts for 2 model pairs, and a one-paragraph written justification naming your 2 finalists.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the model-selection rule before tuning (ship the simpler model unless the challenger beats it by more than a fixed margin), tune both finalists (a logistic-regression C grid and a randomized-search random forest), and choose the contact policy using only out-of-fold training probabilities, never the test set. Open the sealed test set exactly once to compute precision@10% with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval, check it against all 3 written acceptance criteria from the overview chapter, and build the 5-bin calibration table.
slots.deliverable: The tuning results for both finalists with your pre-written selection rule applied, the training-only contact-policy derivation, and a one-time test-set evaluation (precision@10% with its bootstrap interval) checked against every acceptance criterion, plus the calibration table.

slots.practicalActivity: Explain your final model 3 ways: standardized logistic-regression coefficients, permutation importance computed on held-out data, and SHAP values, confirming all 3 agree that order rate, tenure, and late/refunded share are the top drivers. Then test the lesson's hypothesis that tenure is a proxy for accumulated bad deliveries by adding a cumulative bad-order-count feature and re-running cross-validation, checking whether average precision improves and whether tenure's coefficient rank falls once the new feature is included.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side comparison of the 3 explanation methods' top drivers, plus the before/after cross-validated average-precision and coefficient-ranking comparison testing the tenure-as-proxy hypothesis.

slots.practicalActivity: Save the fitted pipeline with joblib, write a model_card.json (version, feature lists, break-even probability, capacity fraction, test metrics, library versions), and write a score_customers() function that rejects input with missing or wrong-typed columns. Build the FastAPI /score endpoint with a Pydantic schema enforcing the exact plan/region/channel literal values, test it with the golden examples plus a deliberately malformed request, and run score_batch.py over the full active-customer table to produce a real contact list capped at the capacity fraction.
slots.deliverable: A saved model artifact with its model_card.json, a tested scoring function and API that passes the golden-example checks and rejects the bad request, and a generated contact-list CSV from a real batch-scoring run.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement psi_numeric(), psi_categorical(), and a full drift_report(), run it as a control against the untouched test set (confirming PSI stays low across every feature) and against a simulated "next quarter" with order-rate, late-share, and plan shifts (confirming the top features correctly alarm). Compute score-PSI and the share of customers above break-even for both scenarios, then simulate the 60-day label lag by scrambling your strongest feature and measuring how far precision@10% falls, confirming why performance monitoring is still needed even when input drift looks clean.
slots.deliverable: A control-vs-shifted drift report with alert/watch/ok status per feature, the matching score-PSI and share-above-break-even comparison, and the scrambled-feature precision drop proving input monitoring alone is not enough.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute cross-validated out-of-fold predictions across all 3,690 active customers, build the risk-decile table (size, churn rate, lift, cumulative capture) and its bar chart with the average-customer and break-even reference lines, then run the value-sensitivity grid across 5 save rates and 3 customer values to stress-test your recommendation's own assumptions. Write the one-slide executive summary and the full slide-by-slide deck outline (ask, problem, approach, evidence, drivers, value, limitations, plan, appendix).
slots.deliverable: The decile table and chart with lift and break-even lines, the 5x3 value-sensitivity grid, a written one-slide executive summary, and a complete slide-by-slide deck outline ready to build into real slides.

slots.practicalActivity: Prepare the answer/evidence/concede/next-step response for all 6 documented pushbacks (is the number good, overfitting or leakage, why not a simpler or fancier model, does the list treat groups fairly, does the offer actually work, will it hold up next quarter), running the real supporting code for each: the train/cross-validation/test AUC comparison, the 3-way rule comparison and its net-per-cycle figures, the precision-on-list table broken down by plan/region/age band, and the randomized-pilot sample-size calculation per arm.
slots.deliverable: A written 4-part response to all 6 pushbacks, each backed by numbers you computed yourself, plus the calculated pilot sample size per arm for testing whether the retention offer's save rate holds up.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite at least 5 of your own resume bullets from the capstone and earlier path courses using the action + metric + tool pattern with a real baseline comparison (not a bare accuracy number), and lay out a one-page resume following the documented section order. Write a searchable LinkedIn headline and 3-paragraph About section. Then build your Harvest Table GitHub repository: a README covering problem, approach, results, limits and how-to-run; the suggested folder layout (data/, sql/, notebooks/, src/, reports/); and run the full pre-publish checklist (no secrets, data rights, synthetic-data disclosure, cleared notebook outputs, no large files, a license).
slots.deliverable: 5 rewritten before/after resume bullets, a complete one-page resume draft, a LinkedIn headline and About section, and a publish-ready GitHub repository that passes every item on the pre-publish checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Map your own 4-week interview-prep plan against the documented round sequence (recruiter screen, team conversation, SQL/coding, statistics/ML, case or take-home, onsite loop, behavioral, offer), and write your 60-second pitch naming the Harvest Table project. Then work through all 11 of the lesson's statistics-and-ML interview questions in your own words, running at least 3 of the supporting code snippets yourself: the max_depth bias-variance comparison, the SelectKBest leakage-vs-pipeline demonstration (0.83 leaky vs. 0.49 proper), and the A/B-test peeking simulation (14.2% vs. 5.1% false-positive rate).
slots.deliverable: A written 4-week prep plan with your rehearsed 60-second pitch, and your own idea/example/caveat answers to all 11 interview questions, with the 3 supporting code runs and their reproduced numbers.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's small practice database (customers, orders, and a raw_customers table with duplicates) by hand in SQLite, then solve all 4 classic interview patterns from scratch without looking at the example answers: top-N-per-group with ROW_NUMBER, deduplicate-keep-latest-record, cohort retention with a LEFT JOIN, and days-since-previous-order with LAG, checking each result against a hand calculation on your tiny dataset. Re-solve the same 4 problems in pandas and confirm both routes agree exactly.
slots.deliverable: Your own from-scratch SQL solutions to all 4 practice patterns with hand-verified results, plus matching pandas solutions for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a fresh churn-style prompt and talk through the lesson's 8-step outline out loud (clarify the decision, define the target precisely, check the data for leakage, start with a baseline, validate honestly, choose action-tied metrics, translate into business value, state limits and next steps), running the net_value() cost calculation with your own illustrative inputs at 2 different capture-rate scenarios. Then time-box a 2-hour mock take-home write-up on the same prompt, following the documented habits: reproducible code, a simple baseline before anything fancy, and an honest limits section.
slots.deliverable: A full worked 8-step case response for a new prompt with your own net_value() comparison at 2 capture rates, plus a 2-hour time-boxed mock take-home write-up with a README and stated assumptions.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 real STAR stories from your own capstone and course work (a metrics judgment call, a problem you caught, a simplification you made, a limitation you disclosed), and rehearse explaining your churn model to a non-technical audience using the decision-first pattern (what it does, how it compares to a baseline, what it cannot do, the recommended next step). Then research a realistic entry-level data-scientist salary range for your target city from at least 2 sources, and run the total_comp() comparison across 3 hypothetical offers to confirm, as the lesson's own numbers show, that the highest base salary is not always the highest total package.
slots.deliverable: 4 written STAR stories with situation/task/action/result, a rehearsed one-paragraph non-technical model explanation, a researched salary range with its sources, and a 3-offer total-compensation comparison table.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, and the Data Scientist path as a whole, a graduate can take a messy, real-world-shaped business dataset from a vague stakeholder request all the way through SQL extraction, Python cleaning, exploratory analysis, a leakage-safe model with honestly evaluated and explained results, a packaged and monitored deployment, and a defended stakeholder presentation — and can walk into a data science interview with a polished resume, a publish-ready GitHub portfolio, and rehearsed answers across SQL, statistics, case-study, and behavioral rounds.
